method: remote camera traps (Reconyx Hyperfire H500, P800 and P900 on trees at 1 m, facing game trails or open areas); daily activity patterns per season from detections; overlap with bison estimated as coefficient D4
conditions: Free-ranging elk inside fenced Elk Island National Park, Alberta, Canada (2.2 m perimeter fence; elk density 3-4 per km2 from aerial surveys; translocations no longer allowed and no elk removed during the study). 43 camera sites, 43,076 camera days pooled across the north (EINP-N) and south (EINP-S) sections; elk detections 5,790 (summer, 19,764 camera days), 2,690 (fall, 8,568) and 2,407 (winter, 14,744). The paper analyses the two park sections pooled and names the species Cervus elaphus; the MDD accepts the North American elk as Cervus canadensis. Bison in the same paper are not filed (plains and wood bison pooled).

source.title: Bison and elk spatiotemporal interactions in Elk Island National Park

quote: Elk activity patterns were clearly crepuscular across seasons.
note: Licence sentence read on the Frontiers PDF: 'This is an open-access article distributed under the terms of the Creative Commons Attribution License (CC BY).' Byline (two authors) read on the same PDF. Category is the paper's own wording. Methods print no scientific name for elk; the Abstract and Introduction use Cervus elaphus, the MDD species page (Cervus canadensis Erxleben, 1777, split from C. elaphus) opened. Animals live in a fenced, managed park: free-ranging inside the fence, not captive; two park sections pooled in the analysis.
